reading.body:
Khosla Ventures led the first venture capital investment in OpenAI's for-profit entity, committing 50 million dollars in January 2019, establishing an early foothold in AI infrastructure funding.

Vinod Khosla's investment thesis connects two eras of computing. Sun Microsystems, which he co-founded in 1982, built the servers and infrastructure that enabled the internet to scale. Khosla Ventures, founded in 2004, shifted his focus to experimental technologies with broad reach. The OpenAI investment in 2019 arrived before the transformer scaling laws were widely understood and before compute constraints became central to AI progress. This was venture capital betting on an unproven team and approach, not yet bidding up valuations based on power and facilities requirements.

The 50 million dollar investment represented an early bet on AI as a technology domain worthy of dedicated capital, but the data does not cover the subsequent rounds of funding OpenAI raised, the expansion of Khosla Ventures' AI portfolio, or the firm's positioning as the power and grid constraints became binding on the industry. It shows the entry point, not the long-term strategy or returns.

standing.watch: What remains unresolved in the records is the litigation. Every listed case, from TradeSun, Inc. v. OpenAI OpCo, LLC to Vredenburgh v. OpenAI OpCo, LLC, is recorded only as filed, with docket monitoring active and no development recorded yet by this tracker. The records give no outcome, no ruling and no settlement for any of them. They also give no planned listing, no valuation and no funding figure beyond the 50 million dollar investment in OpenAI in January 2019. On the question of what comes next for Khosla himself, the records are thin and say nothing further.
standing.record: The site's records for Khosla add up to two companies and a set of lawsuits. The companies are Khosla Ventures, founded in 2004 in Menlo Park, California, and OpenAI, founded in 2015 in San Francisco, in which Khosla Ventures invested. The lawsuits listed are TradeSun, Inc. v. OpenAI OpCo, LLC, Bass v. OpenAI, LLC, United States v. OpenAI OpCo LLC, Buist v. Anthropic, PBC, JIANG v. OPENAI GROUP PBC, Smigelski v. OpenAI OpCo, LLC, GRANT v. OPENAI INC, and Vredenburgh v. OpenAI OpCo, LLC. Each is recorded as filed with docket monitoring active and no development recorded yet by this tracker. The pattern running through the record is that Khosla's presence in artificial intelligence is tied to OpenAI, both through the 2019 investment and through the many cases naming OpenAI entities, while one case names Anthropic rather than OpenAI.
standing.standing: Vinod Khosla stands in artificial intelligence as the founder of Khosla Ventures, the firm he established in 2004, and as a co-founder and the founding CEO of Sun Microsystems in 1982. Through Khosla Ventures he holds influence over an investment portfolio that the records describe as including OpenAI, the startup founded in 2015. The records state that in January 2019 Khosla Ventures led a 50 million dollar investment in OpenAI, becoming the first venture firm to invest in the company. They also state that he held a stake described as approximately 5 percent of OpenAI's for-profit entity following that investment. Beyond these holdings, the records show no other role, control or position for him in artificial intelligence.
